subject: Architecture
title: The Vdara Hotel: Another Death Ray
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Vdara Hotel: Another Death Ray.

hook.text: Las Vegas built a curved glass hotel that scorched pool guests — the same mistake London would make years later.

buildup.text: The Vdara Hotel's concave glass tower focuses desert sunlight onto the swimming pool deck below.

discovery.text: Guests reported singed hair, melted plastic bags, and second-degree sunburns in concentrated hot spots.

twist.text: The architects had identified the risk during design but believed window film would solve it. It didn't.

climax.text: Staff now deploy extra umbrellas and move lounge chairs away from the 'death ray' zone during peak hours.

punchline.text: Curved glass in the desert. Someone should have seen this coming.

quiz.question: How does the Vdara Hotel manage its solar reflection problem?
options: The building was demolished and rebuilt with flat glass
Staff deploy extra umbrellas and relocate chairs from hot spots
Robotic screens automatically block reflected sunlight

details.summary: The Vdara Hotel in Las Vegas, designed by Rafael Viñoly who also designed the Walkie Talkie, created a similar death ray effect. Its curved glass tower focused sunlight onto the pool deck below, creating a hot spot that singed guests' hair and melted plastic pool furniture.
details.whyItMatters: Vdara shows that the same architect repeated a solar reflection mistake across two buildings. It highlights how architectural design can fail when physics modeling is overlooked, even by prestigious firms.
takeaways: Vdara's curved glass focused sunlight into a pool deck hot spot
The same architect later repeated the mistake at London's Walkie Talkie
Solar reflection modeling became a critical design requirement

faq.question: How hot did the Vdara death ray get?
faq.answer: Pool area temperatures reportedly spiked to nearly 67°C (152°F) in the focused beam. Guests reported singed hair, melted plastic bags, and burning sensations. The hotel now provides extra shading, but the architectural lesson about curved glass facades was learned the hard way.

faq.question: Why did the same architect repeat the mistake?
faq.answer: Rafael Viñoly's Vdara opened in 2009, before the London Walkie Talkie (2014). Both used concave glass facades that acted as parabolic reflectors. The Walkie Talkie was already under construction when Vdara's problem became public, making redesign difficult.
